In standard benign operation, the system prompt $S$ guides the distribution toward an approved task domain $\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}$:

An adversary crafts an adversarial perturbation $\delta \in \mathcal{V}^*$ appended to user query $X$ designed to maximize the probability of an unauthorized target output $Y_{\text{target}}$ (e.g., emitting harmful advice or revealing $S$):

In continuous gradient-based attacks (such as GCG: Greedy Coordinate Gradient), the attacker approximates discrete token replacements using the gradient of the loss with respect to one-hot token embeddings:

### 3.2 Information-Theoretic Bounds on Instruction Bounding
Why is it mathematically impossible to achieve 100% prompt injection immunity purely through prompt engineering (*"Never let the user override your rules"*)?
We prove this via the **Unified Modality Indistinguishability Theorem**.
Let $S = (s_1, \dots, s_k)$ and $X = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ be sequences of tokens residing in shared vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$. The input to the transformer is the concatenated sequence:
$$Z = S \circ X = (z_1, z_2, \dots, z_{k+n})$$
The transformer computes attention activations through pairwise token affinities:
$$\mathbf{A}_{i, j} = \frac{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$$
Notice that for any token $z_i$, its query vector $\mathbf{q}_i$ interacts identically with key $\mathbf{k}_j$ regardless of whether index $j \le k$ (system token) or $j > k$ (user token). The positional embeddings encode relative or absolute distance, not privileged cryptographic provenance.
Therefore, there exists a non-zero probability that an input $X$ can produce internal attention representations that mimic or exceed the attention mass of $S$:
$$\exists X \in \mathcal{V}^* \quad \text{such that} \quad \sum_{j > k} \mathbf{A}_{i, j} \gg \sum_{j \le k} \mathbf{A}_{i, j}$$
**Corollary**: Perfect, mathematical immunity to prompt injection cannot be achieved within the autoregressive attention layer alone. It requires **Architectural Defense-in-Depth**: 1. Pre-execution input classification firewalls, 2. Deterministic XML delimiter escaping, 3. Post-execution canary leak detectors, and 4. Programmatic output assertion gates.
### 3.3 Loss Landscape Geometry of Adversarial Suffixes
In empirical research on adversarial robustness (Zou et al., 2023), the loss landscape of autoregressive models with respect to adversarial token permutations exhibits **extreme non-convexity with sharp local minima**.
Let $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ce}}(\delta)$ denote the cross-entropy loss of the target jailbreak output. Unlike smooth vision models where adversarial perturbations can be found via simple projected gradient descent (PGD), discrete text optimization requires navigating a discrete combinatorial hypercube $\{0, 1\}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times T}$.
The transferability of adversarial suffixes across model architectures (e.g., an attack suffix computed on Llama 2 transferring successfully to GPT-4 or Claude 3.5) occurs because foundation models trained on similar large-scale web text share **convergent latent geometry in early representation layers**:
$$\cos\left( \mathbf{v}_{\text{llama}}(\delta), \mathbf{v}_{\text{gpt}}(\delta) \right) \approx 0.72$$
Because internal representation spaces converge, prompt hardening cannot rely on proprietary obscurity; it must implement structural input sanitation.
### 3.4 The Safety-Utility Pareto Frontier & False Refusal Calibration
A critical challenge in adversarial prompt hardening is **Over-Defensiveness (Benign Utility Erosion)**.
As prompt engineers introduce aggressive negative injunctions (*"Under no circumstances mention passwords, keys, or security vulnerabilities"*), the model begins falsely refusing legitimate, benign user requests (e.g., a software developer asking *"How do I securely store user passwords using bcrypt in Django?"*).
We model this tradeoff along a **Pareto Frontier**:
$$\max_{\mathcal{P}} \left( \mathcal{R}_{\text{safe}}(\mathcal{P}), \mathcal{U}_{\text{benign}}(\mathcal{P}) \right)$$
Subject to:
$$\mathcal{F}_{\text{false\_refusal}}(\mathcal{P}) = 1 - \mathcal{U}_{\text{benign}}(\mathcal{P}) \le \epsilon_{\text{allowable}}$$
Where $\mathcal{R}_{\text{safe}}$ represents the fraction of adversarial attacks successfully repelled, and $\mathcal{U}_{\text{benign}}$ represents the utility score on harmless domain inquiries.
If an over-zealous security policy drives $\mathcal{F}_{\text{false\_refusal}} > 0.05$ (a 5% false refusal rate), business users abandon the AI platform in frustration or construct their own shadow workarounds, increasing overall enterprise operational risk.
Calibrating prompts requires evaluating both adversarial test sets and massive benign contrastive datasets simultaneously.
